R001.text: Fix x∈ℝ^n and t>0, and let j be any spatial index with 1≤j≤n when considering a spatial derivative. For any use of a source requiring a curve on all ℝ, extend the time curve by zero at nonpositive times. This extension agrees on a neighborhood of every positive time, so its derivatives there are unchanged by the definition of derivative. By H002 all the coordinate curves and derivatives used here are differentiable near this interior point. H004 gives u(x,r)·u(x,r)=1 for r near t. Apply M007 over ℝ with both curves r↦u(x,r) and both derivatives u_t(x,t). The derivative of the constant right side is zero, while that of the left side is 2u(x,t)·u_t(x,t). Thus u·u_t=0 at (x,t). The same argument along any spatial coordinate gives u·∂_{x_j}u=0. These identities hold throughout the open domain.

Choose a from H005 at (x,t). Using F001, u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu)=u_t·(a u)=a(u_t·u)=0, without differentiating a. For completeness retain the explicit equation from the supplied proof. Differentiate the identities u·u_t=0 and u·∂_{x_j}u=0 once more along their respective coordinate curves. M007 gives u·u_tt=−|u_t|² and u·∂_{x_jx_j}u=−|∂_{x_j}u|². Dotting u_tt−Δ_xu=a u with u and using H004 gives a=∑_j|∂_{x_j}u|²−|u_t|². The same algebra applies to every scalar satisfying the normality equation, not just the chosen witness.

By H002, derivatives of every order are continuous; finite inner products and finite sums of their components are smooth, so e is smooth. To identify its time derivative, apply M008 over ℝ to u locally at (x,t), with order 2. One may extend u arbitrarily outside the open domain: all derivative statements are local and the point has a neighborhood wholly in the domain. Evaluate symmetry on the time direction and the jth spatial coordinate direction. These evaluations of the second Fréchet derivative are respectively ∂_t∂_{x_j}u and ∂_{x_j}u_t, hence they agree. Apply M007 to the time curves u_t and u_t, and to ∂_{x_j}u and itself for each index; differentiating the finite sum defining e now gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2∑_j∂_{x_j}u·∂_{x_j}u_t. It is continuous by H002. F001 and F002 and these identities hold for arbitrary x,t; universal introduction proves the full output.

R002.text: Fix t0>0 and put J=[t0/2,3t0/2]. Both endpoints are positive and the left is strictly smaller than the right. H006 therefore supplies a compact spatial set on which the perturbation may be supported throughout J.
Choose C as in F001. Apply M006 with real codomain to the continuous Euclidean norm on C. It gives a real upper bound for |x| on C, including when C is empty.

Choose L from F002 and set R=max(1,L+1), Q=[−R,R]^n. Then R>0 and for x∈C every coordinate satisfies |x_j|≤|x|≤L<R. Thus C⊂(−R,R)^n=int Q. H001 ensures the stated positive finite dimensions; Q is a compact product of closed bounded intervals. For the coordinate product Lebesgue measure its measure is the finite product ∏_{j=1}^n(2R)=(2R)^n<∞.

The set (ℝ^n\C)×int J is open, since compact C is closed in Euclidean space. There u is identically the fixed q by F001. At every point of this open set all positive-order coordinate derivatives vanish: the first derivative is the limit of zero difference quotients in a neighborhood, and repetition proves the assertion at every finite order. H002 gives continuity of all derivatives everywhere on the time-domain. Therefore, at any r∈int J, every spatial function in the output's list is continuous and zero off C; its nonzero set has closure contained in the closed compact C. Apply M005 to each of these functions. This proves all their integrability claims, including e(·,t0), e_t and every product used later. Equivalently, each is bounded in absolute value on Q by M006 and has absolute integral at most that bound times (2R)^n.

The closed time interval [3t0/4,5t0/4] lies in int J. The product Q×[3t0/4,5t0/4] is compact. H002 implies that e_t is continuous there, since e is a finite sum of squares of smooth component derivatives. Apply M006 to |e_t| on this space-time compact box to obtain a finite real upper bound.

Choose B0 as in F005 and put B=max(0,B0). Then B≥0 and the same bound holds with B. F003 and F004 give all the claimed support, measure and integrability assertions. In particular t0∈int J. Since t0 was arbitrary, e(·,t) is integrable at every positive time; the witnesses C,R,B establish the full more precise assertion.

R003.text: Fix t0>0 and choose the compatible witnesses C,R,B from N002. Set Q=[−R,R]^n and η=t0/4. Then [t0−η,t0+η]=[3t0/4,5t0/4]⊂(t0/2,3t0/2). N002 proves |e_t|≤B on the corresponding space-time box. N001 gives that r↦e(x,r) is differentiable at each point of this interval with derivative e_t(x,r). For every x∈Q and 0<|h|<η, apply M004 on this real convex interval with endpoints t0,t0+h. It yields |e(x,t0+h)−e(x,t0)|≤B|h|. Outside Q both densities are zero by N002, since C⊂int Q. Therefore the absolute difference quotient is ≤B1_Q(x) for every x∈ℝ^n.

Define bnd(x)=B1_Q(x). Q is closed and has finite measure (2R)^n by N002. M009 with constant B and set Q gives integrability of B on Q. Extending this restricted constant by zero off the measurable Q is exactly bnd, so bnd is integrable on ℝ^n.

Define F(h,x) as the difference quotient for 0<|h|<η and zero otherwise. For these small nonzero h, its spatial section is continuous by N001 and is integrable by N002 and linearity of integrability. Hence it is a.e. strongly measurable. At every fixed x the difference quotients tend, as h→0 through h≠0, to e_t(x,t0), by N001. F001 and F002 give an integrable bound for the punctured germ. Apply M001 to Lebesgue measure on ℝ^n, scalar codomain ℝ, parameter h∈ℝ with filter 𝓝[≠]0, F as just defined, f(x)=e_t(x,t0), and bound bnd. The filter is countably generated, with the punctured intervals 0<|h|<1/k for positive integers k as a countable neighborhood basis. Consequently ∫F(h,x)dx→∫e_t(x,t0)dx along that filter.

N002 discharges the guard for E and gives integrability of e(·,t0+h) and e(·,t0) at the nearby positive times, as well as of e_t(·,t0). For 0<|h|<η, linearity of the integral gives ∫F(h,x)dx=(E(t0+h)−E(t0))/h. F003 is therefore exactly the difference-quotient criterion for differentiability of this finite real-valued E: E'(t0)=∫e_t(x,t0)dx. Substitute the full e_t identity from N001. Every summand is integrable by N002. H002 ensures the derivative notation has its usual classical meaning on the open time-domain. Since t0 was arbitrary, this proves the full differentiation assertion.

R004.text: Fix t0>0 and an index 1≤j≤n. Choose compatible C,R from N002 and put Q=[−R,R]^n and g(x)=u_t(x,t0)·∂_{x_j}u(x,t0). H002 makes g smooth. N002 gives g=0 off C and C⊂int Q, so g vanishes on a neighborhood of the boundary of Q (the open complement of C contains that boundary). Apply M007 along the jth coordinate to u_t and ∂_{x_j}u at time t0. This gives ∂_{x_j}g=∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u+u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u. Each term is continuous and integrable by N002.

For each fixed choice of the remaining n−1 coordinates in [−R,R], consider the scalar function of x_j obtained by restricting g to that coordinate line. It is smooth on ℝ, including both endpoints −R and R. Its derivative is continuous and hence integrable on this compact interval, and the function has zero value at both endpoints because these points lie on the boundary of Q, outside C. M002 therefore gives ∫_{−R}^{R} ∂_{x_j}g dx_j=0. To make the product identification explicit, define split(x)=(x_j,(x_k)_{k≠j}) with the other coordinates ordered increasingly. Insertion at position j is its inverse, as is checked coordinate by coordinate. Since 1≤j≤n, one has n=(n−1)+1. Apply M010 with d=n−1, every coordinate space ℝ, every coordinate measure the Lebesgue measure restricted to [−R,R], and selected index j (converted to zero-based Fin n). Each coordinate measure is finite, hence sigma-finite. The source gives that split is a measure-preserving measurable equivalence between Lebesgue measure restricted to Q and the product of the jth restricted coordinate measure with the restricted product of the other coordinates; the original product of restrictions is the restriction of dx to Q because both agree on coordinate rectangles. Thus transport by split takes the integrable function ∂_{x_j}g on Q to its composition with insertion, with the same integral and integrability for this product measure. Now M003 integrates the selected first factor in the inner integral. The FTC equality just proved makes that inner integral zero at every choice of the remaining coordinates in their box. Hence ∫_Q ∂_{x_j}g dx=0. When n=1 the remaining coordinate space is a singleton with empty product measure of mass one, so the same argument reduces to the FTC equality. Endpoints do not affect the Lebesgue interval integral since singletons have zero measure.

All terms of F001 vanish outside Q by N002, since C⊂int Q. Thus their integrals over Q equal their whole-space integrals. Integrate the equality in F001 and use F002 and linearity for the integrable summands: 0=∫_{ℝ^n}∂_{x_j}u_t·∂_{x_j}u dx+∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx. Symmetry of the real dot product and subtraction give precisely the asserted integration-by-parts identity, including finiteness of both sides. Since t0 and j were arbitrary this proves the output.

R005.text: Fix t0>0. N002 proves integrability of e(·,t0) and all the products below and discharges the guard for the actual finite E. N003 gives differentiability and the integral of the full e_t identity. Sum the integration-by-parts identity N004 over the finite spatial indices and substitute it to obtain E'(t0)=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·u_tt dx−2∑_{j=1}^n ∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·∂_{x_jx_j}u dx=2∫_{ℝ^n}u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu) dx. Here H002 makes the component derivatives well-defined and D002 is precisely the finite componentwise sum. Integral linearity applies because N002 gives integrability of every summand.

By N001 the integrand in F001 is identically zero, so its integral is zero and E'(t0)=0. The choice of t0 was arbitrary. Together with integrability from N002 and differentiability from N003 this proves all the requested pointwise-in-time assertions on (0,∞).

For the constancy asserted in the supplied proof, fix any a,b>0. On S=[min(a,b),max(a,b)] all times are positive. F002 gives differentiability of E at every point of S and |E'|≤0 there. Apply M004 over ℝ with c=0, ξ=a, ζ=b to get |E(b)−E(a)|≤0|b−a|=0, hence E(b)=E(a). This includes a=b. Substituting D003 and D004 shows the exact normalization in P, with no factor 1/2; all times used are strictly positive and no value or assertion at time zero was introduced.
